clinicalPearls: Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase normally remethylates homocysteine to methionine using betaine as the methyl donor, mainly in the liver and kidney
It provides the folate-independent, vitamin B12-independent alternative to the methionine synthase remethylation route
A deficiency would be expected to raise plasma total homocysteine while leaving methionine low or normal, resembling other remethylation defects
This is the enzyme therapeutically exploited when betaine is given in classical homocystinuria and severe MTHFR deficiency
An isolated human deficiency remains, at most, extremely rare and is not a firmly established clinical entity
Hyperhomocysteinaemia in practice is far more often due to nutritional deficiency, CBS or MTHFR defects, or cobalamin disorders
If suspected, diagnosis would rest on plasma homocysteine and amino acids with exclusion of the common causes, followed by BHMT genetic analysis
Any treatment would follow generic remethylation-defect principles, ensuring adequate betaine substrate and folate/cobalamin sufficiency
reference.pathophysiology: Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase catalyses transfer of a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, regenerating methionine and producing dimethylglycine. This pathway operates chiefly in the liver and kidney and works in parallel with the folate- and cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase route, offering an alternative means of disposing of homocysteine and replenishing methionine. In principle, loss of this activity would reduce remethylation capacity and allow homocysteine to accumulate, with methionine tending to be low or normal. Because the parallel methionine synthase pathway can compensate, and because a distinct human deficiency has not been clearly delineated, the clinical consequences of isolated BHMT deficiency remain largely theoretical.
additionalDifferentials: Cobalamin remethylation defects such as cblC and cblE
Nutritional vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Methionine synthase and methionine synthase reductase defects
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids to exclude methylmalonic aciduria
BHMT gene analysis where an isolated defect is genuinely suspected after exclusion of common causes
redFlags: Markedly raised homocysteine with thromboembolic events
Failure to identify a common cause after thorough workup
Rapid change during catabolic stress in a patient with unexplained hyperhomocysteinaemia
reference.prognosis: Because a distinct human deficiency is not well established, a defined natural history cannot be given; any hyperhomocysteinaemia attributable to reduced BHMT activity would be expected to respond to correction of the underlying imbalance and adequate remethylation support.
pitfalls: Diagnosing BHMT deficiency before excluding the far commoner causes of hyperhomocysteinaemia
Treating it as a securely defined clinical entity when the human phenotype is uncertain
Overlooking nutritional and renal contributions to a raised homocysteine
Confusing the therapeutic role of betaine, which acts through this enzyme, with a primary enzyme deficiency
references: Mudd SH et al. Homocysteine and its disulfide derivatives review
Huemer M et al. Guidelines for remethylation disorders
management: No established disease-specific therapy; support the parallel folate- and cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase remethylation route with vitamin B12 and folate
Correct any coexisting nutritional deficiency of folate, vitamin B12 and vitamin B6 as the common, treatable causes of raised homocysteine
Exclude and treat the far more likely cystathionine beta-synthase, MTHFR and cobalamin disorders before attributing hyperhomocysteinaemia to this enzyme
Monitor plasma total homocysteine and methionine to gauge response to remethylation support
Referral to metabolic medicine and clinical genetics for confirmation and management of a genuinely suspected isolated defect
Genetic counselling for presumed autosomal recessive inheritance if a defect is confirmed
